content: Preterm infants diagnosed with respiratory distress syndrome (RDS) are at a heightened risk of experiencing negative neonatal and developmental outcomes. In animal studies, thyroid hormones have been shown to promote the production of surfactant and decrease both the incidence and severity of respiratory distress when administered before birth. This study aimed to evaluate whether postnatal administration of thyroid hormone therapy in preterm infants with suspected RDS leads to meaningful clinical improvements in respiratory health and subsequent neonatal and long-term outcomes. To address this, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including The Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), MEDLINE, PREMEDLINE, and EMBASE, covering studies up to March 2006. Additional sources such as previous reviews, cross-references, conference proceedings, and expert consultations were also utilized. The inclusion criteria focused on trials involving preterm infants with suspected RDS who were treated with thyroid hormones within the first 48 hours after birth, compared to a control group. The quality of the trials was independently assessed by the authors, and data were extracted and analyzed using standard Cochrane Collaboration methods. The results were synthesized using relative risk (RR) and weighted mean difference (WMD). Two studies met the inclusion criteria. The first study (Amato, 1988) administered L-thyroxine at a dose of 50 μg at 1 hour and 24 hours after birth, while the second study (Amato, 1989) provided L-triiodothyronine at a dose of 50 μg/day in two divided doses over two days. Both studies had significant methodological limitations, including quasi-randomized allocation of participants, lack of blinding in treatment and outcome measurement, and considerable loss of participants after allocation. Neither study demonstrated significant benefits of thyroid hormone therapy in reducing neonatal morbidity or mortality. A meta-analysis of the two studies, which included a total of 80 infants, found no significant difference in mortality rates prior to discharge (RR 1.00, 95% CI 0.47 to 2.14). The 1988 study reported no significant reduction in the need for mechanical ventilation (RR 0.64, 95% CI 0.38 to 1.09). Additionally, no significant effects were observed in other outcomes, including the duration of mechanical ventilation, incidence of air leaks, chronic lung disease (CLD) at 28 days in survivors, patent ductus arteriosus, intraventricular hemorrhage, or necrotizing enterocolitis. Neurodevelopmental outcomes were not reported in either study. In conclusion, there is no evidence from controlled clinical trials to support the use of postnatal thyroid hormone therapy in reducing the severity of respiratory distress syndrome, neonatal morbidity, or mortality in preterm infants with RDS.
